claim: At the time of birth, zebrafish are mostly quiescent but in response to a tactile stimulus exhibit crude locomotor behaviors that entail powerful and large bends of the body such as seen during escape and struggle.
source: At the time of birth, a zebrafish is mostly quiescent but in response to a tactile stimulus exhibits crude locomotor behaviors that entail powerful and large bends of the body such as seen during escape and struggle (Figure 1A, Escape, Struggle) (McLean and Fetcho, 2009; Liao and Fetcho, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to McLean and Fetcho, 2009 and Liao and Fetcho, 2008, and reference to Figure 1A showing these behaviors.

claim: Early-born behaviors (escape and struggle) require strong activation of axial muscles across a large portion of the fish's body despite their differences with respect to the direction of motion and tail beat frequency.
source: This indicates that both of these early-born behaviors require strong activation of axial muscles across a large portion of the fish's body despite their differences with respect to the the direction of motion and tail beat frequency (escape is forward locomotion with fast tail beat frequency while struggle is backward locomotion with slow tail beat frequency).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that both behaviors involve powerful whole-body bends.

claim: By 2 days after birth, zebrafish spontaneously exhibit a more refined locomotor behavior wherein only the caudal portion of the tail moves with relatively weaker and slower wave-like undulating movements.
source: However, by 2 days after birth, the fish also spontaneously exhibit a more refined locomotor behavior wherein only the caudal portion of the tail moves (Figure 1A, Spontaneous swim) with relatively weaker and slower wave-like undulating movements (McLean and Fetcho, 2009, Figure 1A; Mirat et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to McLean and Fetcho, 2009 and Mirat et al., 2013, and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Tail-restricted locomotion allows the fish to move forward by keeping its head, and therefore gaze, stable.
source: With this type of tail-restricted locomotion, the fish is able to move forward by keeping its head, and therefore gaze, stable.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation of tail-restricted movements.

claim: The ability to keep gaze stable may be critical for the subsequent development of visually guided behaviors such as prey capture.
source: This ability may be critical for the subsequent development of visually guided behaviors such as prey capture.
evidence: Speculative statement about the functional significance of stable gaze.

claim: Escape, one of the crude locomotor patterns that emerge early after the birth of a zebrafish, is controlled by spinal interneurons that are born well before the animal's birth.
source: Escape, one of the crude locomotor patterns that emerge early after the birth of a zebrafish, is controlled by spinal interneurons that are born well before the animal's birth (McLean and Fetcho, 2009; Kimura et al., 2006; Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to McLean and Fetcho, 2009; Kimura et al., 2006; Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012.

claim: The more refined and weaker locomotion pattern that emerges after an animal's birth is controlled by spinal interneurons that are born around the time of an animal's birth.
source: whereas the more refined and weaker locomotion pattern that emerges after an animal's birth is controlled by spinal interneurons that are born around the time of an animal's birth (McLean et al., 2007; Satou et al., 2012; McLean and Fetcho, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to McLean et al., 2007; Satou et al., 2012; McLean and Fetcho, 2009.

claim: The sequential emergence of new and more sophisticated locomotor patterns during development is mediated at the level of the spinal cord by the addition of distinct functional groups of neurons rather than by fine control of a single functional group.
source: This indicates that the sequential emergence of new and more sophisticated locomotor patterns during development is mediated at the level of the spinal cord by the addition of distinct functional groups of neurons rather than by fine control of a single functional group (Fetcho and McLean, 2010).
evidence: Inference based on the observation that different locomotor patterns are controlled by neurons born at different times, supported by citation to Fetcho and McLean, 2010.

claim: In the mammalian spinal cord, distinct functional groups emerge in sequence during development.
source: Similarly in the mammalian spinal cord, it has been shown more recently that distinct functional groups emerge in sequence during development (Tripodi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tripodi et al., 2011.

claim: Locomotion-related signals from the brain reach the spinal cord by way of excitatory reticulospinal neurons of the hindbrain.
source: Locomotion-related signals from the brain reach the spinal cord by way of excitatory reticulospinal neurons of the hindbrain (Dubuc et al., 2008; Grillner and Georgopoulos, 1996; Jordan et al., 2008; Roberts et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dubuc et al., 2008; Grillner and Georgopoulos, 1996; Jordan et al., 2008; Roberts et al., 2008.

claim: V2a neurons in the hindbrain are glutamatergic and project their axons ipsilaterally.
source: V2a neurons in the hindbrain, similar to the ones in the spinal cord, are glutamatergic and project their axons ipsilaterally (Cepeda-Nieto et al., 2005; Kinkhabwala et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2013; Bouvier et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cepeda-Nieto et al., 2005; Kinkhabwala et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2013; Bouvier et al., 2015.

claim: Hindbrain V2a neurons include excitatory reticulospinal neurons and are capable of initiating and terminating locomotion.
source: They include excitatory reticulospinal neurons (Cepeda-Nieto et al., 2005; Kimura et al., 2013; Bouvier et al., 2015) and are capable of initiating and terminating locomotion (Kimura et al., 2013; Bouvier et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cepeda-Nieto et al., 2005; Kimura et al., 2013; Bouvier et al., 2015.

claim: Hindbrain V2a neurons in larval zebrafish show a topographical organization related to differentiation time such that newly-born neurons stack dorsally to pre-existing ones.
source: Interestingly, the hindbrain V2a neurons in larval zebrafish show a topographical organization that is related to differentiation time such that newly-born neurons stack dorsally to pre-existing ones (Kinkhabwala et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kinkhabwala et al., 2011.

claim: In a subset of hindbrain V2a neurons, the ventral, early-born population gets recruited during escape-like locomotion with fast tail beat frequency while the dorsal, late-born population gets recruited during spontaneous swim-like locomotion with slow tail beat frequency.
source: Furthermore, in a subset of the hindbrain V2a neurons, it has been shown that the ventral, and therefore early-born, population gets recruited during escape-like locomotion with fast tail beat frequency while the dorsal, and therefore late-born, population gets recruited during spontaneous swim-like locomotion with slow tail beat frequency (Kinkhabwala et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kinkhabwala et al., 2011.

claim: In the case of midbrain descending pathways, the recruitment of spinal neurons is determined not by selectivity of the descending inputs these neurons receive but by the biophysical properties they express.
source: Indeed, in the case of midbrain descending pathways, the recruitment of spinal neurons is determined not by selectivity of the descending inputs these neurons receive but by the biophysical properties they express (Wang and McLean, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and McLean, 2014.

claim: At 24 hpf, one or two pairs of V2a neurons appeared in a segmental fashion in the hindbrain.
source: At 24 hpf, one or two pairs of V2a neurons appeared in a segmental fashion (Figure 1B iii, iii', 24 hpf)
evidence: Observation from time lapse imaging shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of hindbrain V2a neurons increased dramatically until 60 hpf.
source: and then the number of V2a neurons increased dramatically until 60 hpf (Figure 1B iii, iii', 60 hpf).
evidence: Observation from time lapse imaging shown in Figure 1B.

claim: After 72 hpf, the hindbrain V2a cluster showed no drastic visible changes in the overall shape.
source: After 72 hpf, the V2a cluster showed no drastic visible changes in the overall shape (Figure 1B iii, iii', 72–120 hpf).
evidence: Observation from time lapse imaging shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The connectivity of hindbrain V2a neurons and their electrophysiological properties need to mature to support refined locomotion.
source: As a fish is still only capable of generating crude forms of locomotion at 72 hpf, this suggests that the connectivity of its neurons and their electrophysiological properties need to mature to support refined locomotion.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that neurogenesis is complete before refined locomotion appears.

claim: In most rhombomeres, V2a neurons born by 24 hpf were located in the most lateral portions of the brain region occupied by this group of neurons.
source: In most rhombomeres, V2a neurons born by 24 hpf were located in the most lateral portions of the brain region occupied by this group of neurons (Figure 2—figure supplements 1C and 24 hpf conversion, magenta cells)
evidence: Observation from photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: V2a neurons born after 24 hpf gradually filled up the space medial to the pre-existing ones.
source: whereas neurons born afterwards gradually filled up the space medial to the pre-existing ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and 36–72 hpf conversion).
evidence: Observation from photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Photoconversion at 72 hpf revealed relatively few, if any, unconverted green cells, except in the rostral hindbrain, indicating that the neurogenesis of hindbrain V2a neurons was mostly complete by 72 hpf.
source: Compared to photoconversion at earlier time points, photoconversion at 72 hpf revealed relatively few, if any, unconverted green cells, except in the rostral hindbrain (Figure 2—figure supplements 1C and 72 hpf conversion). This indicated that the neurogenesis of hindbrain V2a neurons was mostly complete by 72 hpf
evidence: Observation from photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The dorsal subpopulation of reticulospinal neurons (MiD2i, MiD3i, RoM2, RoM3 and dorsal MiV1) corresponded to V2a neurons born by 24 hpf.
source: The dorsal subpopulation of reticulospinal neurons (Figure 2C, MiD2i, MiD3i, RoM2, RoM3 and dorsal MiV1) corresponded to V2a neurons born by 24 hpf (Figure 2D)
evidence: Observation from photoconversion and backfill experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The majority of ventral reticulospinal neurons (RoV3, ventral MiV1 and MiV2) corresponded to V2a neurons born by 36 hpf.
source: while the majority of ventral reticulospinal neurons (RoV3, ventral MiV1 and MiV2) corresponded to V2a neurons born by 36 hpf (Figure 2E; Video 2).
evidence: Observation from photoconversion and backfill experiments shown in Figure 2E and Video 2.

claim: The birth order of reticulospinal neurons identified by photoconversion is consistent with previous birthdating analysis based on the incorporation of a marker into replicating DNA.
source: This birth order is consistent with previous birthdating analysis of reticulospinal neurons based on the incorporation of a marker into replicating DNA (Mendelson, 1986).
evidence: Comparison with previous study cited as Mendelson, 1986.

claim: In the caudal hindbrain, the cell bodies of the earliest-born V2a neurons were located lateral to the populations born afterwards.
source: In this region, the cell bodies of the earliest-born V2a neurons were located lateral to the populations born afterwards (Figure 2F).
evidence: Observation from photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The caudal hindbrain contained the youngest group of neurons among the hindbrain V2a descending neurons examined, suggesting their roles in the refined locomotion that develops later.
source: Notably, this region contained the youngest group of neurons among the hindbrain V2a descending neurons we examined, suggesting their roles in the refined locomotion that develops later (Figures 2F and 48 hpf conversion).
evidence: Inference based on the observation that these neurons are born late, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The optical backfill at 36 hpf labeled the dorsal V2a but not the ventral V2a reticulospinal neurons.
source: The optical backfill at 36 hpf labeled the dorsal V2a but not the ventral V2a reticulospinal neurons (Figure 3C)
evidence: Observation from optical backfill experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The optical backfill at 60 hpf labeled both the dorsal and ventral reticulospinal neurons, indicating that these neurons had projected to the rostral spinal cord in sequence based on their respective differentiation times.
source: while the backfill at 60 hpf labeled both the dorsal and ventral reticulospinal neurons (Figure 3D), indicating that these neurons had projected to the rostral spinal cord in sequence based on their respective differentiation times.
evidence: Observation from optical backfill experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The sequential development of spinal projections based on differentiation time holds true for the caudal hindbrain V2a subpopulation.
source: The V2a subpopulation in the caudal hindbrain showed a pattern similar to that indicated by the birthdating analysis (Figure 3E). This indicates that the sequential development of spinal projections based on differentiation time holds true for the caudal hindbrain V2a subpopulation as well.
evidence: Observation from optical backfill experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The caudal medial V2a neurons had descending processes in the rostral spinal cord by 84 hpf, suggesting they contribute to the refined locomotion that appears as early as 96 hpf.
source: As these neurons had descending processes in the rostral spinal cord by 84 hpf, it is plausible that they contribute to the refined locomotion that appears as early as 96 hpf.
evidence: Inference based on the timing of spinal projection development relative to the appearance of refined locomotion.

claim: The birth order of hindbrain V2a neurons dictated the positions of their cell bodies and the order of their spinal projections.
source: Furthermore, we found that the birth order of these neurons dictated the positions of their cell bodies and the order of their spinal projections.
evidence: Summary of findings from developmental analysis.

claim: Fish at 120-132 hpf spontaneously exhibited episodes of rhythmic axial motor activity with maximum beat frequencies that matched those of slow spontaneous swims in unparalyzed fish.
source: In this condition, fish spontaneously exhibited episodes of rhythmic axial motor activity (Figure 4A i; Figure 4B i). The maximum beat frequencies of these episodes matched those of slow spontaneous swims generated through tail-restricted movements in unparalyzed fish (12 fish, Figure 4C) (Mirat et al., 2013); Marques et al., 2018), suggesting that these episodes are fictive analogs of refined locomotor behavior.
evidence: Observation from paralyzed fish experiments shown in Figure 4, compared with previous studies cited as Mirat et al., 2013 and Marques et al., 2018.

claim: Transient electrical pulse delivered to one side of the head evoked locomotor episodes similar to escapes in unparalyzed condition.
source: The first paradigm made use of a transient electrical pulse delivered to one side of the head to evoke locomotor episodes similar to escapes in unparalyzed condition (Figure 4A i).
evidence: Observation from paralyzed fish experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Putative escape episodes started with strong axial motor activity on the side contralateral to stimulation, consistent with the powerful whole-body bending away from the stimulus observed at the start of escape.
source: These episodes started with strong axial motor activity on the side contralateral to stimulation, which is consistent with the powerful whole-body bending away from the stimulus observed at the start of escape (Liu and Fetcho, 1999; Koyama et al., 2016).
evidence: Observation from paralyzed fish experiments, consistent with previous studies cited as Liu and Fetcho, 1999 and Koyama et al., 2016.

claim: Maximum beat frequencies during putative escape episodes were significantly higher than those during spontaneous rhythmic activity.
source: Maximum beat frequencies during these episodes was also significantly higher than those during spontaneous rhythmic activity (Figure 4C, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Gradual mechanical stimulus applied to the front of the head evoked locomotor episodes similar to struggles.
source: The second paradigm employed a gradual mechanical stimulus applied to the front of the head to evoke locomotor episodes similar to struggles (Liao and Fetcho, 2008).
evidence: Observation from paralyzed fish experiments, with citation to Liao and Fetcho, 2008.

claim: Putative struggle episodes exhibited powerful bursting activity consistent with the powerful whole-body bending observed during struggles.
source: These episodes exhibited powerful bursting activity (Figure 4B i), consistent with the powerful whole-body bending observed during struggles (Liao and Fetcho, 2008).
evidence: Observation from paralyzed fish experiments shown in Figure 4B, with citation to Liao and Fetcho, 2008.

claim: The maximum beat frequencies of putative struggles were clearly lower than those of putative escapes and also statistically lower than those of spontaneous slow swims.
source: The maximum beat frequencies of these powerful bouts of bursting activity were clearly lower than those of putative escapes (Figure 4C, p<0.001) and also statistically lower than those of spontaneous slow swims (Figure 4C, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The early-born group (<24 hpf) did not show any clear response during spontaneous weak swimming, but many neurons in this group showed significant responses during putative struggles and even stronger responses during putative escapes.
source: The early-born group (Figure 4C,<24 hpf) did not show any clear response during spontaneous weak swimming, but many neurons in this group showed significant responses during putative struggles that exhibited strong locomotor activity but with low beat frequency. The responses in a few of these neurons were even stronger during putative escapes that exhibited strong locomotor activity with high beat frequency (Figure 4C, MiD2i, RoM2 and RoM3).
evidence: Observation from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The intermediate-aged group (24-36 hpf) showed mixed recruitment patterns: the subgroup in the rostral hindbrain showed comparably strong activity during putative escapes and putative struggles but not during weak spontaneous swims, whereas the subgroup in the middle hindbrain showed comparably strong activity in all three conditions.
source: On the other hand, the intermediate-aged group (Figure 4C 24-36 hpf) showed mixed recruitment patterns; the subgroup in the rostral hindbrain (Figure 4C, RoV3) showed comparably strong activity during putative escapes and putative struggles but not during weak spontaneous swims whereas the subgroup in the middle hindbrain (Figure 4C, ventral MiV1) showed comparably strong activity in all three conditions.
evidence: Observation from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The late-born group in the caudal hindbrain (36-60 hpf) showed more activity only during weak spontaneous swimming and showed decreased activity during stimulus-evoked strong swims.
source: In contrast, the late-born group in the caudal hindbrain (Figure 4C 36-60 hpf) showed more activity only during weak spontaneous swimming. Interestingly, during stimulus-evoked strong swims, these neurons showed decreased activity instead, raising the possibility of inhibition during strong swims.
evidence: Observation from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A recruitment pattern based on the time of differentiation holds true for all the hindbrain V2a descending neurons identified based on development: the early-born group is recruited during the crude forms of locomotion (escapes and struggles) that appear early in development whereas the late-born group is recruited during the refined locomotion that appears later in development.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that a recruitment pattern that is based on the time of differentiation holds true for all the hindbrain V2a descending neurons that we identified based on development; the early-born group is recruited during the crude forms of locomotion (escapes and struggles) that appear early in development whereas the late-born group is recruited during the refined locomotion that appears later in development.
evidence: Summary of findings from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The activity map for shock-evoked putative escapes revealed a large population of recruited neurons on the side contralateral to the stimulus, including the dorsal early-born group and the rostral intermediate group (RoV3) in the rostral hindbrain and a large number of the lateral early-born neurons in the caudal hindbrain.
source: The activity map for the shock-evoked putative escapes (Figure 5A iii, left; Figure 5A iv, magenta; Video 4, magenta) revealed a large population of recruited neurons on the side contralateral to the stimulus (ipsilateral to the leading side of motor activity), consistent with their primarily ipsilateral projections (Kinkhabwala et al., 2011). This includes the dorsal early-born group and the rostral intermediate group (RoV3) in the rostral hindbrain (Figure 5A v, magenta) and a large number of the lateral early-born neurons in the caudal hindbrain (Figure 5A vi, magenta).
evidence: Observation from regression analysis shown in Figure 5A and Video 4, with citation to Kinkhabwala et al., 2011.

claim: The activity map for spontaneous weak swimming revealed the middle intermediate group (ventral MiV1) in the rostral hindbrain and a large number of the medial late-born neurons in the caudal hindbrain.
source: The activity map for spontaneous weak swimming revealed the middle intermediate group (ventral MiV1) in the rostral hindbrain (Figure 5A iii, right; Video 4, green) and a large number of the medial late-born neurons in the caudal hindbrain (Figure 5A iii, right; Figure 5A vi, cyan; Video 4, green).
evidence: Observation from regression analysis shown in Figure 5A and Video 4.

claim: The activity maps for putative escapes and struggles were surprisingly similar, especially in the caudal hindbrain, supporting the idea that the early-born population contributes to the crude whole-body movements observed in both struggles and escapes.
source: The activity maps for putative escapes and struggles were surprisingly similar, especially in the caudal hindbrain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). This supports the idea that the early-born population contributes to the crude whole-body movements observed in both struggles and escapes.
evidence: Observation from regression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The activity of the early-born group is further enhanced during escapes compared to struggles, especially in the rostral hindbrain, suggesting that further activation of this population leads to fast cyclic movements of the whole-body, as observed in escapes.
source: However, this analysis also made it clear that the activity of the early-born group is further enhanced during escapes compared to struggles, especially in the rostral hindbrain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting again that further activation of this population leads to fast cyclic movements of the whole-body, as observed in escapes.
evidence: Observation from regression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The neuropil active during weak spontaneous swimming was located lateral to the neuropil active during putative struggles in the caudal hindbrain, and this functional segregation is the opposite of the functional segregation of cell bodies.
source: The neuropil active during weak spontaneous swimming was located lateral to the neuropil active during putative struggles (Figure 5B vi, filled arrowheads; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Struggle, arrowheads). This functional segregation is the opposite of the functional segregation of cell bodies in the caudal hindbrain (Figure 5B vi, open arrowheads).
evidence: Observation from regression analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The neuropil from V2a neurons born before 24 hpf was located medial to the neuropil from neurons born after 24 hpf in the hindbrain and throughout the spinal cord.
source: In the hindbrain (Figure 6A iii), and throughout the spinal cord (Figure 6A iv-vi), the neuropil from V2a neurons born before 24 hpf (Figure 6A iii-vi, magenta arrowheads) was located medial to the neuropil from neurons born after 24 hpf (Figure 6A iii-vi, green arrowheads)
evidence: Observation from photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The neuropil from V2a neurons born before 36 hpf was still located medial to the neuropil from neurons born after 36 hpf, but it extended more toward the lateral surface than the neuropil from V2a neurons born before 24 hpf.
source: The neuropil from V2a neurons born before 36 hpf was still located medial to the neuropil from neurons born after 36 hpf (Figure 6A viii-xi, arrowheads). However, it extended more toward the lateral surface than the neuropil from V2a neurons born before 24 hpf (Figure 6A xii).
evidence: Observation from photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Axonal processes from new V2a neurons were continuously being added laterally to preexisting processes, forming layers based on the time of differentiation.
source: This suggested that axonal processes from new neurons were continuously being added laterally to preexisting processes, forming layers based on the time of differentiation.
evidence: Inference based on the observation of neuropil organization.

claim: The descending processes from the early-born and intermediate-aged hindbrain V2a groups reached the caudal part of the spinal cord and were in the medial part of the neuropil in the rostral and middle spinal cord.
source: The descending processes from the early-born and intermediate-aged groups reached the caudal part of the spinal cord (Figure 6B v) and were in the medial part of the neuropil in the rostral and middle spinal cord (Figure 6B iii-iv, magenta arrowheads).
evidence: Observation from hindbrain photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The descending processes from almost all hindbrain V2a neurons covered almost all the neuropil region formed by V2a neurons.
source: To visualize the spinal projections from almost all the hindbrain V2a neurons, we photoconverted Kaede in the hindbrain at 96 hpf and imaged them at 120 hpf (Figure 6Bvi-ix, n = 8 fish). The descending processes from hindbrain V2a neurons covered almost all the neuropil region formed by V2a neurons (Figure 6B vii-ix, magenta arrowheads).
evidence: Observation from hindbrain photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The descending processes from the late-born group were most prominent in the lateral neuropil in the rostral and middle spinal cord.
source: Comparison of the lateral extents of the descending processes of the early-born and intermediate-aged groups (Figure 6B x, blue lines) and all groups (Figure 6B x, orange lines) indicated that the descending processes from the late-born group were most prominent in the lateral neuropil in the rostral and middle spinal cord.
evidence: Observation from hindbrain photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The spinal projections from hindbrain V2a neurons were layered based on the time of differentiation and the late-born group had shorter descending processes than the early-born and intermediate-aged groups.
source: Taken together, these results indicated that the spinal projections from hindbrain V2a neurons were also layered based on the time of differentiation and that the late-born group had shorter descending processes than the early-born and intermediate-aged groups.
evidence: Summary of findings from hindbrain photoconversion experiments.

claim: The difference in the axon length across different age groups is consistent with the pattern previously revealed by single-cell labeling.
source: The difference in the axon length across different age groups is consistent with the pattern previously revealed by single-cell labeling (Kinkhabwala et al., 2011).
evidence: Comparison with previous study cited as Kinkhabwala et al., 2011.

claim: Primary motoneurons (PMN) were located close to the medial neuropil region occupied by the spinal projections from the early-born hindbrain V2a population.
source: We found that PMNs were located close to the medial neuropil region occupied by the spinal projections from the early-born hindbrain V2a population
evidence: Observation from photoconversion and backfill experiments.

claim: Multipolar commissural neurons (MCoDs) were located close to the lateral neuropil region occupied by the spinal projections from the late-born population.
source: whereas MCoDs were located close to the lateral neuropil region occupied by the spinal projections from the late-born population.
evidence: Observation from photoconversion and backfill experiments.

claim: Direct activation of PMNs throughout the spinal cord by the early-born group is expected to lead to the powerful whole-body bends observed during the crude and strong forms of locomotion (escape and struggle).
source: direct activation of PMNs throughout the spinal cord by the early-born group is expected to lead to the powerful whole-body bends observed during the crude and strong forms of locomotion (escape and struggle)
evidence: Inference based on the connectivity pattern of the early-born group.

claim: Indirect activation of SMNs in the caudal spinal cord through MCoDs should lead to slow bending of the caudal tail observed during the more refined and weaker locomotion.
source: whereas indirect activation of SMNs in the caudal spinal cord through MCoDs should lead to slow bending of the caudal tail observed during the more refined and weaker locomotion.
evidence: Inference based on the connectivity pattern of the late-born group.

claim: In rhombomere 4, newly generated V2a neurons were systematically located ventral to preexisting ones.
source: We found that newly generated V2a neurons were systematically located ventral to preexisting ones (Figure 7B iii)
evidence: Observation from photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The inverted organization of V2a neurons in rhombomere 4 was due to radial migration.
source: To see if this inverted organization was due to migration, we performed time lapse imaging from 25 hpf to 37 hpf (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, n = 6) and from 48 hpf to 78 hpf (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, n = 6). We found that newly generated neurons were indeed initially located dorsal to preexisting ones (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A iii) but the subpopulation of neurons born before 48 hpf migrated ventrally after 48 hpf (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B iii, magenta cells; Video 6). This supported the idea that the inverted organization we observed in this region was indeed due to radial migration.
evidence: Observation from time lapse imaging shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Video 6.

claim: The dorsally located early-born MiV1 neurons showed strong depolarization leading to action potentials during the fastest phase of fast swim episodes evoked by electrical shock to the tail, but showed no clear depolarization during spontaneous slow swim episodes.
source: The dorsally located early-born MiV1 neurons (n = 8, position: 0.14–0.18) showed strong depolarization leading to action potentials during the fastest phase of fast swim episodes evoked by electrical shock to the tail (Figure 7C ii, left orange traces, shaded cycle). However, they showed no clear depolarization during spontaneous slow swim episodes (Figure 7C ii, right orange traces).
evidence: Observation from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The middle MiV1 neurons showed clear spiking activity at the fastest phase of the shock-induced fast swimming and also showed clear rhythmic depolarization leading to occasional firing during spontaneous slow swimming.
source: The middle MiV1 neurons that belong to the intermediate age group (n = 13, position: 0.30–0.48) showed clear spiking activity at the fastest phase of the shock-induced fast swimming. They also showed clear rhythmic depolarization leading to occasional firing during spontaneous slow swimming (Figure 7C ii, green traces).
evidence: Observation from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The ventral late-born MiV1 neurons showed clearly rhythmic firing during both shock-induced fast swimming and spontaneous slow swimming.
source: The ventral late-born MiV1 neurons (n = 23, position: 0.64–0.93) showed clearly rhythmic firing during both shock-induced fast swimming and spontaneous slow swimming (Figure 7C ii, blue traces).
evidence: Observation from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Spiking activity showed clear statistical interaction between the time of differentiation and the speed of locomotion, suggesting that groups of neurons that differed by age were recruited differently depending on the speed of locomotion.
source: Spiking activity showed clear statistical interaction between the time of differentiation and the speed of locomotion (Figure 7D, p<0.001), suggesting that groups of neurons that differed by age were recruited differently depending on the speed of locomotion.
evidence: Statistical analysis of whole-cell recording data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Subthreshold activity showed similar interaction between the time of differentiation and the speed of locomotion, suggesting that this recruitment pattern can be explained at least partly by their distinct synaptic inputs.
source: Subthreshold activity also showed similar interaction (Figure 7E, p<0.001), suggesting that this recruitment pattern can be explained at least partly by their distinct synaptic inputs.
evidence: Statistical analysis of whole-cell recording data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The MiV1 group showed systematic differences in their intrinsic excitability based on their time of differentiation: the older neurons showed lower input resistances and more hyperpolarized membrane potentials compared to younger ones.
source: At the same time, the MiV1 group showed systematic differences in their intrinsic excitability based on their time of differentiation: the older neurons showed lower input resistances and more hyperpolarized membrane potentials compared to younger ones (Figure 7F, Rin, Vrest).
evidence: Observation from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The older MiV1 neurons showed faster membrane time constants than the younger ones.
source: Furthermore, we also found a systematic change in the membrane time constants: the older neurons showed faster membrane time constants than the younger ones (Figure 7F, Tau).
evidence: Observation from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 7F.

claim: All the cells in the early-born dorsal MiV1 group had clear puncta-like structures in close proximity to the somata of PMNs and SMNs but not spinal V2a neurons.
source: All the cells in this group had clear puncta-like structures - putative presynaptic terminals - in close proximity to the somata of PMNs (Figure 8B iv, 8 out of 8 cells) and SMNs (Figure 8B v, 4 out of 4 cells) but not spinal V2a neurons (Figure 8B vi, 0 out of 7 cells).
evidence: Observation from single-cell labeling experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The firing of an action potential in dorsal MiV1 led to a postsynaptic potential in PMN in most pairs.

claim: The longer latency component of the EPSP from dorsal MiV1 to PMN was blocked by a mixture of glutamatergic blockers, leaving only the shorter latency component.

claim: The initial short latency response from dorsal MiV1 to PMN was probably due to an electrical synapse, and the later response that followed this was due to a glutamatergic synapse.
source: Therefore, the initial short latency response was probably due to an electrical synapse, and the later response that followed this was due to a glutamatergic synapse.

claim: None of the MCoDs showed a postsynaptic response to an action potential elicited in the dorsal MiV1.

claim: None of the PMNs showed a postsynaptic response to an action potential elicited in ventral MiV1.

source: while one-third of MCoDs examined showed a clear postsynaptic potential (Figure 9D; 8 out of 21).

claim: The responses in MCoDs from ventral MiV1 persisted in high magnesium and calcium solution, suggesting they were generated monosynaptically.

evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings.

claim: Ventral MiV1s showed selective monosynaptic connectivity to MCoDs, the late-born spinal interneurons that are only active during slow swimming.

source: In seven out of seven cases, a clear biphasic postsynaptic potential was observed in PMNs in response to an action potential in MiD3i (Figure 9E).

evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings.

evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 9E.

claim: In 14 out of 14 cases, PMNs showed very strong postsynaptic potentials leading to spiking activity in response to a single action potential in the M-cell.
source: The M-cell also showed similar, but much stronger connections. In 14 out of 14 cases, PMNs showed very strong postsynaptic potentials leading to spiking activity in response to a single action potential in the M-cell (Figure 9G iii).

claim: The responses from M-cell to PMN persisted in high magnesium and calcium solution, suggesting that the connections were monosynaptic.
source: These responses also persisted in high magnesium and calcium solution, suggesting that the connections were monosynaptic.
evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings.

source: These responses were completely blocked by a cholinergic blocker (Figure 9G iii; n = 10), indicating that they were mediated by cholinergic synapses, in accordance with existing literature (Koyama et al., 2011; Clemente et al., 2004).
evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 9G, with citations to Koyama et al., 2011 and Clemente et al., 2004.

claim: MCoDs showed a long latency complex postsynaptic potential in response to one M-cell action potential, suggesting that the connection is probably polysynaptic.
source: MCoDs on the other hand showed a long latency complex postsynaptic potential in response to one M-cell action potential, suggesting that the connection is probably polysynaptic (Figure 9H iii; 13 out of 13 cases).

source: Most, if not all, of the responses disappeared in high magnesium and calcium solution, further supporting that they are mediated polysynaptically (Figure 9H iii; n = 10).
evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 9H.

claim: Both types of early-born descending neurons make synaptic connections to the early-born PMNs but not to the late-born MCoDs.
source: In sum, our findings indicate that both types of early-born descending neurons make synaptic connections to the early-born PMNs but not to the late-born MCoDs.

claim: The connection probability was statistically different depending on the hindbrain cell type and the spinal cord cell type.

claim: PMNs and MCoDs received synaptic inputs from completely different sets of reticulospinal neurons, with each set corresponding to distinct age group.

claim: Early-born and late-born hindbrain neurons form parallel pathways to the spinal cord and these pathways are organized based on the time of differentiation.
source: Thus, these results showed electrophysiologically that early-born and late-born hindbrain neurons form parallel pathways to the spinal cord and these pathways are organized based on the time of differentiation
evidence: Summary of findings from paired whole-cell recordings.

claim: The youngest ventral MiV1/MCoD pairs were the slowest among the connected pairs in terms of conduction velocity.
source: We first examined differences in conduction velocity among connected pairs (Figure 9J): the youngest ventral MiV1/MCoD pairs were the slowest among the connected pairs.
evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 9J.

claim: The middle-aged pairs (dorsal MiV1/PMN and Mid3i/PMN) were slower than the oldest M-cell/PMN pairs in terms of conduction velocity.
source: The middle-aged pairs (dorsal MiV1/PMN and Mid3i/PMN) were slower than the oldest M-cell/PMN pairs.
evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings.

claim: The youngest ventral MiV1/MCoD pairs showed significantly longer time constants of synaptic potentials than the older V2a neurons.
source: We also examined differences in the time constants of synaptic potentials, excluding the M-cell/PMN pair that showed spiking activity (Figure 9K). The youngest ventral MiV1/MCoD pairs showed significantly longer time constants than the older V2a neurons (Figure 9K).
evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 9K.

claim: The M-cell/PMN pair was the only pair that was statistically different from other pairs with respect to the amplitudes of the synaptic potentials.
source: With respect to the amplitudes of the synaptic potentials, the M-cell/PMN pair was the only pair that was statistically different from other pairs (Figure 9L).
evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 9L.

claim: The early-born PMNs and the late-born MCoDs examined differed significantly in input resistance.
source: However, consistent with previous studies (McLean et al., 2007; Menelaou and McLean, 2012), the early-born PMNs and the late-born MCoDs examined here differed significantly in input resistance (92.3 ± 18.2 M Ohm and 514 ± 172 M Ohm, respectively; Wilcoxon test, p<0.001)
evidence: Observation from paired whole-cell recordings, with citations to McLean et al., 2007 and Menelaou and McLean, 2012.

claim: The underlying synaptic currents were systematically stronger for the early-born hindbrain neurons than the late-born hindbrain neurons.
source: suggesting that the underlying synaptic currents were systematically stronger for the early-born hindbrain neurons than the late-born hindbrain neurons.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that PMNs and MCoDs differ in input resistance.

claim: The early-born pathway is equipped with fast conduction velocities, fast time constants of synaptic potentials and stronger synaptic currents while the late-born pathway is equipped with slow conduction velocities, slow time constants of synaptic potentials and weaker synaptic currents.
source: Altogether, we found systematic differences in conduction velocities, synaptic decay times and synaptic currents between the two parallel pathways: the early-born pathway is equipped with fast conduction velocities, fast time constants of synaptic potentials and stronger synaptic currents while the late-born pathway is equipped with slow conduction velocities, slow time constants of synaptic potentials and weaker synaptic currents.
evidence: Summary of findings from paired whole-cell recordings.

claim: The differences in the biophysical properties as well as connectivity patterns are consistent with the distinct types of axial motor activity observed during the locomotor patterns in which these pathways participate.
source: The differences in the biophysical properties as well as connectivity patterns are consistent with the distinct types of axial motor activity observed during the locomotor patterns in which these pathways participate.
evidence: Inference based on the observed biophysical properties and connectivity patterns.

claim: Activation of early-born pathways could produce more powerful whole body bending observed during different crude forms of locomotion (escape and struggle).
source: As a consequence, activation of early-born pathways could produce more powerful whole body bending observed during different crude forms of locomotion (escape and struggle)(McLean et al., 2008; Liao and Fetcho, 2008)
evidence: Inference based on the connectivity patterns and biophysical properties, with citations to McLean et al., 2008 and Liao and Fetcho, 2008.

claim: Activation of late-born pathways could produce weaker bending of the caudal tail region with a long rostrocaudal delay, as observed during the refined locomotion.
source: whereas activation of late-born pathways could produce weaker bending of the caudal tail region with a long rostrocaudal delay, as observed during the refined locomotion (McLean et al., 2008).
evidence: Inference based on the connectivity patterns and biophysical properties, with citation to McLean et al., 2008.

claim: The parallel hindbrain-spinal cord circuits that develop in sequence and have distinct connectivity patterns and biophysical properties contribute to the distinct locomotor patterns that zebrafish display in sequence.
source: In sum, these results suggest that the parallel hindbrain-spinal cord circuits that develop in sequence and have distinct connectivity patterns and biophysical properties contribute to the distinct locomotor patterns that zebrafish display in sequence.
evidence: Summary of findings from paired whole-cell recordings.

claim: Auditory stimulus-elicited escape episodes consisted of large and fast changes in head orientation as well as body bends, characteristic of the crude locomotion that develops early.
source: Auditory stimulus-elicited escape episodes consisted of large and fast changes in head orientation as well as body bends (Figure 10A ii), these being characteristic of the crude locomotion that develops early.
evidence: Observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Spontaneous swim episodes mostly consisted of small changes in head orientation, and slow and small bends restricted to the caudal portion of the tail, typical of the more refined locomotion that develops later.
source: On the other hand, spontaneous swim episodes mostly consisted of small changes in head orientation, and slow and small bends restricted to the caudal portion of the tail (Figure 10A iii), and these are typical of the more refined locomotion that develops later.
evidence: Observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The distribution of the amplitude of the first total body bend in each spontaneous swim episode was multimodal, suggesting that spontaneous swim episodes consisted of distinct subtypes.
source: Consistent with the findings of a previous study (Burgess and Granato, 2007), when we looked at the distribution of the amplitude of the first total body bend in each spontaneous swim episode we found it to be multimodal, suggesting that spontaneous swim episodes consisted of distinct subtypes (Figure 10A v).
evidence: Observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 10A, with citation to Burgess and Granato, 2007.

claim: A Gaussian mixture model fit indicated that the best fit to the distribution of the first body bend amplitude was using a linear combination of three distinct gaussian distributions, suggesting that there were potentially three subcategories of spontaneous swim episodes.
source: A Gaussian mixture model fit indicated that the best fit to the distribution was using a linear combination of three distinct gaussian distributions, suggesting that there were potentially three subcategories of spontaneous swim episodes (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: For scoots all of the global parameters (total swim distance per episode, maximum swim velocity per episode, mean swim velocity per episode, episode duration, and total number of bends per episode) were significantly reduced in the late-born V2a neuron ablation group.
source: We found that for scoots all of the foregoing global parameters were significantly reduced in the late-born V2a neuron ablation group (Figure 10—figure supplement 2B, p<0.01, corrected for multiple comparisons, Holm test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2B.

claim: For routine turns, ablations of late-born V2a neurons produced a slight reduction in swim distance and mean swim velocity, but at a lower significance level.
source: For routine turns, these ablations produced a slight reduction in swim distance and mean swim velocity, but at a lower significance level (Figure 10—figure supplement 2B, p<0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons, Holm test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Ablation of early-born V2a neurons did not result in changes in any of the global swim parameters.
source: On the other hand, ablation of early-born V2a neurons did not result in changes in any of these global parameters.
evidence: Observation from behavioral experiments.

source: Neither ablation of the early-born or the late-born neurons resulted in a change in the onset latency of escape (Figure 10—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Observation from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2A.

source: Relative to the control group, the early-born V2a ablation group exhibited significant decreases in the amplitudes of the first, second and fourth bends, as well as a decrease in the duration of the first bend of escape (Figure 10C i, Escape; p<0.01, corrected for multiple comparisons, Holm test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The early-born V2a ablation group observed no statistically significant changes in the three other slower locomotor patterns (Scoot, R-turn and High-angle turn).
source: However, we observed no statistically significant changes in the three other slower locomotor patterns (Figure 10C i, Scoot, R-turn and High-angle turn).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 10C.

source: On the other hand, in the late-born V2a ablation group we saw no clear changes in the escape response (Figure 10C ii, Escape).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The late-born V2a ablation group showed a decrease in the amplitudes of bends in the later phase of scoot but not the other two spontaneous swim patterns involving turning.
source: Instead, this group showed a decrease in the amplitudes of bends in the later phase of scoot (Figure 10C ii, Scoot; p<0.01, corrected for multiple comparisons) but not the other two spontaneous swim patterns involving turning (Figure 10C ii, Routine turn and High-angle turn).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Late-born V2a neurons may play a role in maintaining the excitatory drive in the spinal cord during slow forward locomotion.
source: Furthermore, the fact that we observed significant changes only in the late phase of scoots suggests that late-born V2a neurons may play a role in maintaining the excitatory drive in the spinal cord during slow forward locomotion.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that ablation of late-born V2a neurons affected the late phase of scoots.

claim: The ablations did not change the set of distinct locomotor behaviors fish exhibit spontaneously.
source: To summarize, our ablations did not change the set of distinct locomotor behaviors fish exhibit spontaneously.
evidence: Summary of findings from behavioral experiments.

source: In conclusion, with ablation experiments we confirmed our hypothesis about the functional roles of early-born and late-born V2a neurons in freely swimming fish.
evidence: Summary of findings from ablation experiments.

source: Moreover, the double dissociation of the two locomotor patterns indicates that the underlying V2a descending pathways are largely independent, in accordance with their parallel circuit arrangement resulting from the layered growth of their spinal projections.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that ablation of different age groups affected different locomotor patterns.

source: This suggests that the layered development of new connections in the nervous system underlies its ability to integrate new circuits into existing circuitry in such a way as to allow the different circuits to operate autonomously.

source: Interestingly, previous studies showed that the ablation of ventral reticulospinal neurons, the hindbrain V2a neurons we classified as the intermediate-aged group, affects slow but large turns with no clear kinematic effects on forward locomotion and suggested that the descending pathway for turning behaviors is independent of the one for forward locomotion (Huang et al., 2013; Orger et al., 2008).

claim: The array of locomotor behaviors fish display after birth are supported by sequentially developing parallel hindbrain-spinal cord circuits, with each circuit accounting for a specific range of kinematics and dynamics through its unique connectivity pattern and biophysical properties.
source: Collectively, this suggests that the array of locomotor behaviors fish display after birth are supported by sequentially developing parallel hindbrain-spinal cord circuits, with each circuit accounting for a specific range of kinematics and dynamics through its unique connectivity pattern and biophysical properties.

source: Hindbrain V2a descending neurons born early are also the first to project to the spinal cord where they innervate similarly early-born motoneurons throughout the spinal cord with fast conducting axons and synapses that exhibit fast dynamics.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study.

claim: Early-born hindbrain V2a descending neurons contribute to the crude forms of locomotion that consist of powerful bends of the whole-body.
source: Consistent with their connectivity pattern and biophysical properties, they contribute to the crude forms of locomotion that consist of powerful bends of the whole-body.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study.

source: Hindbrain V2a descending neurons born later give rise to a more laterally located layer of descending pathways that function in parallel to existing pathways: through similarly late-born premotor neurons in the rostral spinal cord, these V2a neurons polysynaptically connect to caudal motoneurons via slow conducting axons and synapses that exhibit slow dynamics.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study.

claim: Late-born hindbrain V2a descending neurons contribute to the more refined and weaker locomotion that appears later and that consists of weaker bends of the caudal tail.
source: Consistent with the connectivity pattern and biophysical properties, they contribute to the more refined and weaker locomotion that appears later and that consists of weaker bends of the caudal tail.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study.

claim: The chronological layering of parallel circuits and the systematic variation in the connectivity patterns and biophysical properties of these circuits underlie the diversification and increase in sophistication of the locomotor repertoire.
source: In sum, our results reveal that the chronological layering of parallel circuits and the systematic variation in the connectivity patterns and biophysical properties of these circuits underlie the diversification and increase in sophistication of the locomotor repertoire.

source: Indeed, during the final approach phase of prey capture, zebrafish can increase the speed of forward swimming to values approaching those seen during fast behaviors established earlier in development, but without displaying the large lateral head displacements seen in these earlier-established behaviors (Patterson et al., 2013).

source: Interestingly, the development of the corticospinal pathway in mammals appears to fit into this view; in this pathway, spinal tracts are established postnatally in the lateral part of the spinal cord after the prenatal development of other descending pathways (Lakke, 1997; KUYPERS, 1962), and these tracts contribute to skilled forelimb movements that animals gradually develop postnatally (Martin, 2005; Alstermark and Isa, 2012).

claim: Chronology-based parallel incorporation of new motor circuits provides certain advantages over non-parallel organization.
source: In sum, chronology-based parallel incorporation of new motor circuits provides certain advantages over non-parallel organization.
evidence: Summary of discussion about the advantages of parallel organization.

source: In the lateral line system of zebrafish, sensory afferents in the hindbrain are topologically organized based on their birthdate (Pujol-Martí et al., 2012).

source: The systematic changes in connectivity patterns and biophysical properties we observed in the chronologically layered parallel circuits fit well with the general development pattern of movements observed in many vertebrates (Kagan and Herschkowitz, 2006; Harlow and Harlow, 1965; Fox, 1965; Drapeau et al., 2002).

claim: Correlations between morphological and physiological properties and the time of differentiation have also been reported in the mammalian cortex and hippocampus.
source: Indeed, correlations between morphological and physiological properties and the time of differentiation have also been reported in the mammalian cortex (Butt et al., 2005; Miyoshi et al., 2007) and hippocampus (Picardo et al., 2011; Marissal et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Butt et al., 2005; Miyoshi et al., 2007; Picardo et al., 2011; Marissal et al., 2012.

claim: Systematic changes in morphological and physiological properties represent a general strategy utilized by nervous systems to support the wide range of neural processes required for the complete behavioral repertoire of animals: from the fast and global sensorimotor processing observed in innate reflexive behaviors to the more sustained and finer processing presumed to happen in deliberate and sophisticated cognitive behaviors that animals acquire later.
source: Although the computational and behavioral roles of these systematic changes in morphological and physiological properties remains to be answered, it seems likely that they represent a general strategy utilized by nervous systems to support the wide range of neural processes required for the complete behavioral repertoire of animals: from the fast and global sensorimotor processing observed in innate reflexive behaviors to the more sustained and finer processing presumed to happen in deliberate and sophisticated cognitive behaviors that animals acquire later.
evidence: Speculation about the general significance of systematic changes in morphological and physiological properties.

claim: The hindbrain contains a series of cell types that are arranged in columns that run rostrocaudally throughout the hindbrain.
source: The hindbrain contains a series of cell types that are arranged in columns that run rostrocaudally throughout the hindbrain (Kinkhabwala et al., 2011; Koyama et al., 2011; Gray, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kinkhabwala et al., 2011; Koyama et al., 2011; Gray, 2013.

claim: Each cell type in the hindbrain exhibits a specific combination of transcription factor expression, neurotransmitter identity and axonal projection pattern.
source: Each cell type exhibits a specific combination of transcription factor expression, neurotransmitter identity and axonal projection pattern.
evidence: General knowledge about hindbrain cell types.

claim: It has been proposed that each cell type in the hindbrain may provide a fundamental neural operation that is broadly useful to many sensorimotor circuits.
source: As these cell types span across various sensorimotor circuits in the hindbrain, it has been proposed that each cell type may provide a fundamental neural operation that is broadly useful to many of these circuits (Kinkhabwala et al., 2011; Koyama and Pujala, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kinkhabwala et al., 2011 and Koyama and Pujala, 2018.

claim: There is some evidence suggestive of the involvement of hindbrain V2a neurons in other hindbrain motor circuits besides locomotor circuits.
source: Indeed, there is some evidence suggestive of the involvement of hindbrain V2a neurons in other hindbrain motor circuits besides locomotor circuits.
evidence: General statement about evidence for V2a neuron involvement in other circuits.

claim: In mice, genetic ablation of all V2a neurons in the nervous system produces deficits in respiration.
source: In mice, genetic ablation of all V2a neurons in the nervous system produces deficits in respiration (Crone et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crone et al., 2012.

claim: A class of premotor neurons in the horizontal eye movement circuit partly corresponds to putative V2a neurons in larval zebrafish.
source: A class of premotor neurons in the horizontal eye movement circuit partly corresponds to putative V2a neurons in larval zebrafish (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: Premotor neurons in the horizontal eye movement circuit show persistent activity correlated to eye position but the time constant of persistent activity varies across cells.
source: These neurons show persistent activity correlated to eye position but the time constant of persistent activity varies across cells (Miri et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miri et al., 2011a.

claim: Perhaps one fundamental role of hindbrain V2a neurons is to provide to hindbrain motor circuits a series of excitatory drives that vary in duration so that these circuits can result in a behavioral repertoire containing movements with a wide range of temporal dynamics.
source: Perhaps one fundamental role of hindbrain V2a neurons is to provide to hindbrain motor circuits a series of excitatory drives that vary in duration so that these circuits can result in a behavioral repertoire containing movements with a wide range of temporal dynamics.
evidence: Speculation about the fundamental role of hindbrain V2a neurons.

claim: Previous studies of spinal V2a neurons in larval zebrafish employed tail beat frequency as a readout of locomotor speed and revealed that distinct age groups are recruited as a function of locomotor speed: the early-born group is active during fast locomotion while the late-born group is active during slow locomotion.
source: Previous studies of spinal V2a neurons in larval zebrafish employed tail beat frequency as a readout of locomotor speed and revealed that distinct age groups are recruited as a function of locomotor speed: the early-born group is active during fast locomotion while the late-born group is active during slow locomotion (Kimura et al., 2006; McLean et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kimura et al., 2006 and McLean et al., 2008.

claim: In the context of forward locomotion, the strength of body bends also increases as locomotor speed increases.
source: However, in the context of forward locomotion, the strength of body bends also increases as locomotor speed increases (McLean et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to McLean et al., 2008.

claim: It is possible that spinal V2a neurons are recruited based on the strength of body bends similar to hindbrain V2a descending neurons.
source: Thus, it is possible that spinal V2a neurons are recruited based on the strength of body bends similar to hindbrain V2a descending neurons.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation that body bend strength increases with locomotor speed.

claim: The earlier-born spinal V2a neurons have longer axons than the later-born ones, suggesting that the early-born population contributes to large body bends through its innervation to motoneurons across many segments.
source: Consistent with this idea, the earlier-born spinal V2a neurons have longer axons than the later-born ones (Menelaou et al., 2014), suggesting that the early-born population contributes to large body bends through its innervation to motoneurons across many segments.
evidence: Supported by citation to Menelaou et al., 2014.

claim: The activity of CiD interneurons, putative early-born V2a population, is enhanced when fish exhibit a larger initial bend during escape.
source: Indeed, the activity of CiD interneurons, putative early-born V2a population, is enhanced when fish exhibit a larger initial bend during escape (Bhatt et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2007.

claim: Previous studies in tadpole also identified putative spinal V2a neurons recruited during struggles.
source: Previous studies in tadpole also identified putative spinal V2a neurons recruited during struggles (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: Putative spinal V2a neurons recruited during struggles in tadpole can also fire during fast beat frequencies, suggesting that they correspond to the early-born population active during fast swimming in zebrafish.
source: These neurons can also fire during fast beat frequencies (Li et al., 2007, Figure 4E; Li, 2015, Figure 7A), suggesting that they correspond to the early-born population active during fast swimming in zebrafish.
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2007 and Li, 2015.

claim: Like the hindbrain V2a population examined, spinal V2a neurons may also exhibit recruitment pattern based on the strength of movements.
source: Taken together, this suggests that like the hindbrain V2a population we examined, spinal V2a neurons may also exhibit recruitment pattern based on the strength of movements.
evidence: Inference based on the evidence from zebrafish and tadpole studies.

claim: A shared set of early-born hindbrain V2a descending neurons is recruited during two crude forms of locomotion, struggles and escapes.
source: A shared set of early-born hindbrain V2a descending neurons is recruited during two crude forms of locomotion, struggles and escapes.
evidence: Summary of findings from the study.

claim: The early-born V2a descending pathway is in use during both struggles and escapes and generates strong activation of axial muscles along the whole body as observed in both behaviors.
source: This suggests that the early-born V2a descending pathway is in use during both behaviors and generates strong activation of axial muscles along the whole body as observed in both behaviors.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that the same neurons are recruited during both behaviors.

claim: Within the early-born V2a descending neurons, majority of the cells show stronger activity during escapes.
source: Within the early-born V2a descending neurons, majority of the cells show stronger activity during escapes.
evidence: Observation from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The further recruitment of the early-born pathway underlies the transition from struggles to escapes.
source: This suggests that the further recruitment of the early-born pathway underlies the transition from struggles to escapes.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that more cells are recruited during escapes.

claim: It is possible that non-V2a descending neurons that were not examined in this study show activity only during struggles and recruit spinal neurons active only during struggles such as CoLA.
source: However, it is also possible that non-V2a descending neurons that were not examined in this study show activity only during struggles and recruit spinal neurons active only during struggles such as CoLA (Liao and Fetcho, 2008).
evidence: Speculation about the role of non-V2a descending neurons, with citation to Liao and Fetcho, 2008.

claim: In principle, it is possible for nervous systems to acquire new patterns of activity corresponding to new behaviors through the development of neuromodulatory systems because neuromodulation permits a fixed complement of neurons to give rise to many different patterns of activity.
source: In principle, it is possible for nervous systems to acquire new patterns of activity corresponding to new behaviors through the development of neuromodulatory systems because neuromodulation permits a fixed complement of neurons to give rise to many different patterns of activity (Bargmann, 2012; Marder, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bargmann, 2012 and Marder, 2012.

claim: In larval zebrafish blocking dopamine signaling through D4 receptors leads to less frequent but longer swim episodes.
source: Indeed, in larval zebrafish blocking dopamine signaling through D4 receptors leads to less frequent but longer swim episodes (Lambert et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lambert et al., 2012.

claim: D4 receptor signaling can either suppress or modify the late-born pathway described in this study, suggesting that the development of both new circuits and neuromodulatory systems is required for proper development of locomotor behaviors.
source: Nevertheless, this indicates that D4 receptor signaling can either suppress or modify the late-born pathway we described, suggesting that the development of both new circuits and neuromodulatory systems is required for proper development of locomotor behaviors.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that blocking D4 receptors affects swim episodes.

claim: The parallel arrangement of differentially aged circuits that control distinct behaviors can explain how these behaviors can be controlled independently of one another, but it does not explain how animals can coherently string together these behaviors.
source: Although the parallel arrangement of differentially aged circuits that control distinct behaviors can explain how these behaviors can be controlled independently of one another, it does not explain how animals can coherently string together these behaviors.
evidence: Inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Through their widespread axonal arborizations, early-born 'pioneer' GABAergic neurons in the hippocampus exert a huge impact on the activity of neurons born afterwards, and in this way, these neurons play a crucial role in the synchronization of activity observed in the developing hippocampus.
source: For example, through their widespread axonal arborizations, early-born 'pioneer' GABAergic neurons in the hippocampus exert a huge impact on the activity of neurons born afterwards, and in this way, these neurons play a crucial role in the synchronization of activity observed in the developing hippocampus (Picardo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Picardo et al., 2011.

claim: Early-born 'pioneer' GABAergic neurons in the hippocampus have been shown to exist in the adult hippocampus and to project heavily to the septum.
source: Although these early-born neurons have been shown to exist in the adult hippocampus and to project heavily to the septum (Villette et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Villette et al., 2016.

claim: During escapes, fish transition from fast and crude whole-body movements to slower and refined tail-restricted movements.
source: During escapes, fish transition from fast and crude whole-body movements to slower and refined tail-restricted movements (Mirat et al., 2013; Marques et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mirat et al., 2013 and Marques et al., 2018.

claim: The age-related recruitment pattern observed in V2a descending neurons suggests that neural activity shifts from the early-born neurons contributing to the crude whole-body movements to the late-born reticulospinal neurons contributing to the refined tail-restricted movements.
source: The age-related recruitment pattern we observed in V2a descending neurons suggests that neural activity shifts from the early-born neurons contributing to the crude whole-body movements to the late-born reticulospinal neurons contributing to the refined tail-restricted movements.
evidence: Inference based on the observed recruitment pattern.

claim: The recruitment of the early and late-born reticulospinal neurons are coordinated to ensure the smooth transition from the crude to refined locomotor patterns.
source: This raises the possibility that the recruitment of the early and late-born reticulospinal neurons are coordinated to ensure the smooth transition from the crude to refined locomotor patterns.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed recruitment pattern.

claim: In adult goldfish and zebrafish, it's been shown that the activation of Mauthner cell, the earliest born reticulospinal neuron, influences ongoing slow locomotor activity in the spinal cord, further supporting the presence of coordination between early-born and late-born neurons.
source: Indeed, in adult goldfish and zebrafish, it's been shown that the activation of Mauthner cell, the earliest born reticulospinal neuron, influences ongoing slow locomotor activity in the spinal cord (Svoboda and Fetcho, 1996; Song et al., 2015), further supporting the presence of such coordination.
evidence: Supported by citations to Svoboda and Fetcho, 1996 and Song et al., 2015.
